text: {She} had the build of somebody who had carried coal up four flights and would again.
The block knew {name} as a landlady who never missed a rent day and never forgot a face.
I sit where I can see the stairs. People think that’s nosiness. It’s rent.
Everybody knew {victim}. He came round twice a year about the stairs and the fire escape, and twice a year I paid him not to find anything.
{She} keeps the house, and {she} knows every foot on the stairs.
{He} was a big man going soft.
{He} was the kind of bartender who knew what you drank before you did and never said your name out loud.
I pour and I listen. The pouring is what they pay for.
{He} knows everybody’s drink and nobody’s business.
{She} had the look of somebody who did business standing up, on a curb, with one eye on the street.
On the curb outside the Exchange, {name} was known for a quick yes and a slow no.
Half my customers would rather not be seen buying. I’m what they send instead.
{She} kept both hands still, the way people do whose hands are their living.
The block went to {name} for a tooth when it could pay, and to the barber when it couldn’t.
People are polite to a dentist. They know they’ll be back in the chair.
{He} was the kind of patrolman the block could set a clock by.
